name: Doug Jones
summary: Doug Jones is the Democratic nominee for Alabama governor and a former U.S. Senator. Jones announced plans to temporarily hault new data center projects in the state, running on a platform that includes a one-year moratorium to establish "guardrails." He has expressed opposition to tax breaks for data centers, and did not respond to questions about his stance on reporting requirements for water, utility requirements or noise assessments.

name: Tommy Tuberville
summary: Tommy Tuberville is the Republican challenger for Alabama governor and a sitting U.S. Senator. Tuberville supports data center development in the state, saying that opposition "nonsense" is driven by China and the facilities can foster economic growth in communities that want them. He has taken an anti-tax break stance on the facilities. During the 2026 legislative session, Tuberville sponsored the "Ratepayer Protection Act," which suggested states voluntarily adopt policies to protect consumers and mandate large load facilities pay the total amount for their energy costs. The bill failed in the Senate 57-43.

name: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins
summary: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (JKT) is the sole Democrat running for governor in Alaska. He served in the Alaska House of Representatives from 2013 to 2023 and sevred as a science and technology senior advisor for a New York-based nonprofit. In July he released a platform that would require local approval for data centers to be built, and force AI companies to pay the full cost of their electricity. JKT also proposed a statewide moratorium on future data centers until the Legislature can pass regulatory framework for those developments. He wants to establish laws that prohibit deepfakes used to mislead the public, defend Alaskans from AI-enabled crimes, and hold AI companies liable when their products cause harm. JKT has not clarified whether he supports tax breaks for AI companies if the Legislature enacts guardrails for data center developments.

name: Bernadette Wilson
summary: Bernadette Wilson is the leading Republican in Alaska’s gubernatorial race. She is an entrepreneur and served as senior adviser on U.S. Rep. Nick Begich’s 2024 campaign. Wilson has no information regarding data centers on her campaign website and has limited communication with the press about the topic. In an article published by the Alaska Beacon, she is quoted saying, “I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands.” According to her website, Wilson's main priorities are education and proper distribution of Alaska’s Permanent Fund Dividend.

name: Katie Hobbs
summary: Katie Hobbs, the current governor of Arizona since 2023, is re-running for the position on behalf of the Democratic Party. Besides being a politiician, Hobbs is also a social worker. She was elected to the Arizona House in 2010 and after, served in the Arizona State Legislature for four terms. In 2018, Hobbs was then elected Secretary of State. Hobbs is a big supporter of preserving Arizona's water supply and has pushed to keep water records public. She also spokie on data centers having to pay their share of the costs and does not believe in tax incentives for them. Although Hobbs believes data centers could bring concerns to neighborhoods, she is not pushing for a statewide moratorium.

name: Andy Biggs
summary: Congressman Andy Biggs is currently running for govenor of Arizona on belhalf of the Republican Party. Prior to his election to Congress, Biggs servied in the Arizona State House of Representatives for eight years and the Senate for six years. He is also a retired attorney that has been liscensed to practice in Arizona, New Mexico and Washington. Regarding data centers, Biggs is strongly pushing to end tax incentives for them. He also believes the centers need to produce their own energy to avoid draining Arizona's resources. Along with that, Biggs has a plan to "Accurately measure and report on the state's aquifers" so they have an idea of where Arizona's water levels are at. Similar to his opponent, Biggs also is not pushing for a statewide moratorium of data centers.

name: Frederick Love
summary: Fred Love is a term-limited Arkansas senator running as the Democratic challenger to incumbent Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders.

name: Sarah Huckabee Sanders
summary: Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the incumbent Republican governor of Arkansas who has maintained a data center-friendly environment in the state. Sanders welcomed legislation that created and expanded tax incentives for data centers and has welcomed them to . A spokesperson for Sanders said she helped axe efforts to prevent states from "regulating AI or data centers," but did not directly respond to our questions.

name: Phil Weiser
summary: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser is the Democratic challenger for governor of the state. Weiser has tied his data center stance to the state's climate goals, supporting public reporting requirements for water use. He has rejected imposing a statewide moratorium on the facilities and signaled support for tax incentives in some cases.

name: Victor Marx
summary: Victor Marx is the Republican nominee for Colorado governor. His team did not respond to multiple attempts to reach them for this project.  During an Oct. 8 debate, Marx said he would leave the data center question up to local communities and referred to the facilities as an economic "boost".

name: Ned Lamont
summary: Ned Lamont is the incumbent Democratic governor of Connecticut running for a third term in the 2026 gubernatorial election. He has supported tax incentives for data centers, signing legislation creating the state's incentive program in 2021, although he has since become more critical of large facilities because of their electricity and water demands. Lamont has called for slowing new data centers unless they add power generation and plans to give municipalities more control over siting decisions. I found no clear public position from Lamont on a statewide moratorium, mandatory public water-use reporting or required noise assessments.

name: Ryan Fazio
summary: Ryan Fazio is the Republican challenger for Connecticut governor in 2026 and a state senator representing the 36th District, first elected in 2021. He opposes the state's data-center tax incentives and has proposed repealing them through legislation. Fazio also supports requiring data centers to provide and pay for their own electricity and favors local control over where they are built. I found no clear public position from Fazio on a statewide moratorium, mandatory public water-use reporting or required noise assessments.

name: David Jolly
summary: Former U.S. Rep. David Jolly, a Democrat who previously represented Florida's 13th Congressional District, is running for governor of Florida. Jolly has pledged to implement a one-year statewide moratorium on data center construction to allow further study of environmental and community impacts. He has expressed concerns about data centers' water and electricity consumption and criticized existing tax breaks for developers. Jolly has described Florida's legislation requiring data centers to cover their utility costs as a good first step but argues that additional protections are necessary. He has not explicitly endorsed public water-use reporting requirements, separate utility tariffs or mandatory noise assessments for proposed facilities.

name: Byron Donalds
summary: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds, a Republican representing Florida's 19th Congressional District, is running for governor of Florida. Although his campaign website does not explicitly address data centers, Donalds has publicly supported regulations requiring data centers to cover their own utility costs. He supports Florida's SB 484, which requires large-scale data centers to pay their service costs and establishes water-use requirements. He also introduced federal legislation aimed at preventing data centers from relying on public electricity and water systems. Donalds opposes a statewide moratorium on data centers, instead favoring local control over development decisions. He has not explicitly stated whether he supports public water-use reporting, data center tax incentives or mandatory noise assessments.

name: Keisha Lance Bottoms
summary: Keisha Lance Bottoms is the former mayor of Atlanta running for Georgia governor. She has proposed a moratorium on new data centers to evaluate the cost and environmental impact of the faciilities. She has not said whether she supports public reporting requirements, utility requirements, tax incentives or noise assessments. Her team did not respond to questions for this project.

name: Rick Jackson
summary: Rick Jackson is the Republican challenger for Georgia governor. He has rejected a statewide moratorium in favor of leaving the decision up to local communities. He has proposed a "three part test" emphasizing commnity support, environmental standards and local cost relief. Jackson's campaign did not respond to questions for this project despite multiple attempts to reach them.

name: Josh Green
summary: Josh Green is the incumbent Democratic governor of Hawaii. He has not spoken out publicly about his stance on data center development in the state and his campaign did not respond to multiple attempts to reach them for this project.

name: Gary Cordery
summary: Gary Cordery is the Republican challenger for Hawaii governor. His campaign did not respond to multiple attempts to contact themvia email about his position.

name: Terri Pickens
summary: Terri Pickens is a lawyer and fourth-generation Idahoan running for governor of Idaho as a Democrat. Although she does not have information on her campaign site pertaining to data centers, she is vocal on social media about her stances on data centers. Above all, she wants to protect Idaho's natural resources and does not want to give them away without accountability, according to an Instagram post on her campaign's account. She also said, "As governor, I will require existing AI data centers to publicly report their water and power use, tax breaks, and permanent Idaho jobs. They should pay for the grid upgrades and additional demand they create, including paying for their own power. Special tax treatment should only continue when there is a clear, measurable benefit to Idaho."

name: Brad Little
summary: Brad Little is the incumbent Republican governor of Idaho. He has been serving as governor since 2019 and previously served as an Idaho state senator from 2001-2009, and as Lt. Governor from 2009-2019. Little supports data center projects in Idaho, but wants to conserve resources. He believes data centers should bear their own increased energy costs rather than passing those off to other power users, according to a news release from his office. In 2020, he signed into law a sales tax exemption for data centers, and in 2026, he signed into law a bill to limit the water data centers can use, although their is no public discolsure requirement.

name: JB Pritzker
summary: JB Pritzker is the incumbent governor of Illinois. In June, Pritzker paused all tax incentives for data centers and called on data center reforms. He also urged lawmakers to pass legislation that would require data centers pay for the costs of their energy and water demand, require them to support the generation of renewable energy, to track and report water use, to adhere to air quality standards and to enter agreements with the communities that hosts them. He wants utilities to prioritize residential and regular business customers in times of high energy demand. Prtizker proposed the POWER Act in February but the legislation failed to move out of House and Senate committees before the General Assembly adjourned in the spring. Pritzker has not said whether he supports noise assessment requirements for proposed data centers.

name: Darren Bailey
summary: Darren Bailey is running for governor of Illinois, representing the Republican Party. He was elected to the Illinois House in 2018 and later the State Senate. Bailey feels finding ways to regulate data centers falls back to affordability. While Bailey voices concerns about data centers, his campaign also posts artificial intelligence-generated images on social media. Bailey feels data centers are necessary, but does not support tax incentives for them. Bailey has not said whether he supports public reporting requirements for water use or noise assessment requirements for proposed data centers.

name: Rob Sand
summary: Rob Sand is running for governor of Iowa as a Democrat currently finishing his second tem as State Auditor. In his campaign, he has held strong in the need for regulation on date centers, including introducing water reporting requirements and eliminating tax incentives for data canters. Sand has also proposed forcing data centers to cover utility increases in the community, enacting consumer protetcions and establishing requirements prior to data centers being bult, including public hearings and setback requirements to regulate noise.

name: Zach Lahn
summary: Zach Lahn, the Republican candidate for governor, is a farmer and businessman. He has called for a statewide moratorium on data centers, water use reporting and the elimination of tax breaks for data centers. Lahn has also spoken about proposals to require companies to pay for electricty use and address to environmental concerns.

name: Cindy Hoslcher
summary: Cindy Holscher is the democratic nominee for governor of Kansas. She has expressed supporting a state-wide moratorium on data centers because she believes that the state needs to regulate what companies won’t. She supports public water reporting requirements and separate utility rates for data centers. She previously voted in support of tax incentives to data centers, but has expressed that she changed her mind after listening to constituents. Holscher has not said whether or not she supports noise assessments for data centers.

name: Ty Masterson
summary: Ty Masterson is the republican nominee for governor of Kansas. He has expressed disapproval for a state-wide moratorium on data centers, citing the need for local communities to make decisions for themselves. He has not expressed support for public water reporting for data centers, however he has been involved in Kansas water conservation during his time in the Senate. Masterson previously voted in favor of tax incentives for data centers, and has not changed his position. Masterson has not said whether or not he supports noise assessment requirements for data centers.

name: Hannah Pingree
summary: Hannah Pingree is the Democratic candidate for governor of Maine. She was elected to the Maine House in 2002 and served as the youngest woman and second woman in Maine history to serve as Speaker of the House for a state legislature. In 2019, current Governor Mills tapped her to lead the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future where she worked with issues like housing, labor and economic recovery in Maine. She has alo led the state's Children's Cabinet and Cabinet on Aging as well as climate initiatives. Pingree is a big supporter of enforcing a statewide moratorium on data centers in order to lower issues regarding the environment, health and wellbeing for people living in Maine. She also is a supporter of a moratorium for data centers to cut electricity prices for Maine residents. She has been vocal about her opposition towards current initatives made by Governor Mills regarding data centers, specifically Governor Mills vetoed a legislation that would have enforced a statewide moratorium of data centers. Pingree is an advocate for renewable energy solutions and lowering costs for Maine residents.

name: Bobby Charles
summary: Bobby Charles is the Republican candidate for governor of Maine. He is the former Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs under George W. Bush and founder of The Charles Group, a consulting firm in Washington D.C. His priorities include reducing crime and stoping the drug crisis in the state, enforcing "common-sense policies" on homelessness, making Maine more affordable and holding the state government accountable. There is no mention of data centers on Charles' website, however his stances on this issue derive from local media interviews. Charles supports a statewide moratorium on data centers in order to reduce costs for residents and decreasing environmental impact made by the centers specifically towards rivers in the state. However, Charles opposes renewable energy resources and advocates for natural gas pipelines. It is unclear whether he supports public reporting requirements for water use, as well as tax incentives and noise assessment requirements for proposed data centers.

name: Wes Moore
summary: Wes Moore is Maryland’s current Democratic governor. He doesn't support a statewide moratorium on data centers because he thinks local counties should get to decide that for themselves. But he did sign an executive order in late September putting down state rules to hold data centers accountable. His order sets up a public dashboard to track power and water use, makes companies do noise and community impact reviews, and says data centers have to pay for their own grid upgrades so families aren't hit with higher electric bills. He also wants to get rid of Maryland's 2020 data center sales tax breaks, saying developers need to "pay their own way, or they need to go away"

name: Dan Cox
summary: Dan Cox is the Republican running for Maryland governor. He wants an immediate statewide ban on all data center building because he says they eat up too much power and threaten Maryland’s farms, water, and local towns. In the October debate, Cox pushed back hard on rising energy bills and said everyday residents shouldn't have to foot the bill for power lines or tech companies. He also opposes giving tech developers tax breaks, but he didn't respond to questions about specific water reporting numbers or local noise checks.

name: Maura Healy
summary: In 2023, Maura became the first woman elected Governor in Massachusetts history and the first openly lesbian Governor elected in the country. In her first term in office, Maura has led by building upon what makes Massachusetts special and delivering on her promises to expand opportunities and cut costs.

name: Michael Minogue
summary: Raised as the youngest of four in an Irish Catholic family, Mike chose to attend the United States Military Academy at West Point, driven by a sense of service and patriotism instilled in him by his parents.

name: Jocelyn Benson
summary: Jocelyn Benson is the Democratic challenger in the race for Michigan Governor. She is the current 43rd Michigan Secretary of State. Jocelyn Benson explicitly addresses data centers concerns on her campaign website, promising to put a moratorium on data centers if elected. She emphasizes transparency and guardrails to prioritize the community's best interest before any data centers are built in Michigan. Benson explicity supports bans on data center tax breaks and requiring that they pay for their power. She will ensure public hearings, union contrats for well-paying jobs and that developers prove construction of data centers will not abuse natural resources before building. Waiting on zoning...

name: John James
summary: John James is the current U.S. Representative of Michigan's 10th congressional district. He is a challenger running for Governor under the republican party. James takes a local focus to data centers. He emphasizes that while he generally doesn't support statewide bans as a conservative, data centers won't be built without the community's best interest in mind. He consistenlty says that data center contrusction must protect resources and prevent pollution, but he's unclear on actual requirements. He says that Michigan is open for business but not for sale. Ultimatley, he believes data centers are for to local control.

name: Amy Klobuchar
summary: Amy Klobuchar is the current Democratic representataive for Governor. Klobuchar supports water use in Minnesota as she created the Water Cyber Shield Act with Senator Schiff. Additionally, she was one of four Democratic senators that broke the ranks for the Ratepayer Protection Act; not supporting separating utility rates for data centers. Klobuchar doesn't support tax breaks and wants local Minnesotans to have the final say on data centers. There was no response in regards to zoning.

name: Lisa Demuth
summary: Lisa Demuth is the Republican candidate for Governor. Demuth doesn't directly support water use or focus on envirnomental initatives; however, she was voted on a few environmental bills supporting clean water. Demuth doesn't support having data centers have separate utility bills and wants to increase costs for companies. Additionally, Demuth wants data centers to be on the same playing field as local companies. While supporting tax incentives, Demuth wants to raise taxes and wants to protect taxpayers by adopting new regulations to President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill.

name: Lynne Walz
summary: Lynne Walz is the Democratic candidate and challenger running for Governor of Nebraska. Walz is a born and raised Nebraskan; she started as a caretaker, eventually returning to school and starting her own day care and becoming a 4th and 5th grade teacher. In 2016, she was elected Nebraska legislator and again in 2020. She’s worked hard alongside those with disabilities and law enforcement, earning her the Legislator of the Year from the Fraternal Order of Police. Walz campaign revolves around transparency, affordability, and livable communities.

name: Jim Pillen
summary: Jim Pillen is the Republican candidate and incumbent running for Governor of Nebraska. Pillen is currently the 41st governor of Nebraska, sworn in January 2023. Pillen has a Bachelor’s degree in Animal Science from UNL and a Doctor of Veterinary Medicine from Kansas State University. After graduation, he returned to Nebraska to open his own animal practice, which eventually grew into a family farm business. Pillen’s campaign revolves around tax relief, agriculture, and business growth.

name: Aaron Ford
summary: Aaron Ford has served as Nevada's 34th attorney general since 2019 and is the first African American to hold a statewide constitutional office in Nevada. Ford won the Democratic primary for governor on June 9, 2026. His campaign focused on affordability including housing, health care and energy costs.. Ford declined to state whether he supports a statewide moratorium on data centers. Instead, he has proposed pausing new tax breaks and abatements for data centers while the state audits existing facilities and evaluates their economic impact. Ford supports public reporting and greater transparency surrounding data-center water use. His campaign also says data centers conserve water and bring their own water resources. Ford supports requiring data centers to pay for the energy they consume and the electrical-grid infrastructure needed to serve their facilities. His energy platform says those costs should not be shifted to residential ratepayers. He has also proposed requiring data centers to bring their own clean energy and electrical-grid infrastructure. Ford has not publicly stated whether he supports specific statewide noise-assessment requirements for data centers. His current data-center platform does not explicitly address noise assessments. Ford does not currently support continuing new tax abatements for data centers without further review. He has pledged to pause new abatements while the state determines whether existing incentives have produced the promised economic benefits. Ford supported the 2015 legislation that established Nevada's data-center-tax-break program while serving in the state Senate.

name: Joe Lombardo
summary: Joe Lombardo is the 31st governor of Nevada and was elected in November 2022 after previously serving as Clark County sheriff. Lombardo was elected Clark County sheriff in 2014 and reelected in 2018 before becoming governor. Lombardo has remained supportive of data-center development while seeking additional requirements for facilities receiving state tax incentives. In September 2026, he signed Executive Order 2025-005, establishing new standards for data-center development and requiring facilities seeking partial tax abatements to meet additional conditions involving water, electricity, schools, grid reliability and community impacts. Lombardo does not support a statewide moratorium on data centers. His administration's current policy instead establishes additional guardrails for facilities seeking state tax incentives while continuing to allow data-center development. Lombardo's executive order requires data centers seeking partial tax abatements to meet water standards for their location. The order also requires developers to make commitments concerning water, transparency and community impacts. It additionally calls for annual publication of aggregate information required under the community- support commitments. Lombardo's current data-center policy does not establish a specific statewide noise-assessment requirement. His executive order focuses on water use, electrical-grid reliability, ratepayer protections, school funding, siting and community impacts rather than a separate noise-assessment mandate. Lombardo supports continuing tax incentives for qualifying data centers, but with additional restrictions. His executive order requires facilities seeking partial tax abatements to pay the Local School Support Tax in full and enter into a Nevada Community Support Commitment. The order also allows the state to impose conditions related to water, electricity, grid reliability and community impacts.

name: Cinde Warmington
summary: Cinde Warmington is the democrat challenger to Kelly Ayotte in New Hampshire. On her campaign priorities page, she makes data centers a clear and obvious focus. She states a number of reasons, such as environmental, noise level, and affordable energy bills, why a statewide moratorium would be put in effect if she were elected. Warmington says “New Hampshire still has no guardrails for large-scale data centers. None. No legal definition. No local control. No grid accountability. No noise standards. Not one law on the books to make any developer answer for what they propose to take.” She makes it clear that her issue with data centers in New Hampshire is the lack of regulation. (Note: Warmington has not explicity said that she supports seperate utility rates and use requirements for data centers, although the language on her website heavily suggests so.)

name: Kelly Ayotte
summary: Kelly Ayotte is the incumbent republican governor running for reelection in New Hampshire. Ayotte has recently shifted her stance regarding data centers, and publicly spoke about implementing a statewide moratorium. In the past, she had supported development of data centers but has since agreed that “right now, they do not make sense at all in terms of energy, environment, or location.” In 2025, she had signed a law that allowed for off-grid energy providers in New Hampshire, in an attempt to make the state more attractive to the cryptocurrency industry.

name: Deb Haaland
summary: Deb Haaland is the former secretary of the interior under former President Joe Biden. She is in support of public reporting requirements for water use. According to a campaign handout titled “An Affordable New Mexico” found on her campaign website, she states that as governor she will make sure “water usage is accurately reported each year from traditionally high-demand industries”. Haaland is also in support of separate utility rates and use requirements for data centers. In her eight-point plan for holding data centers accountable, she will require “data centers to build their own renewable energy infrastructure”. Haaland is also in support of a statewide moratorium on data centers, meaning current construction will be halted until the state figures out how to set up protections. Haaland’s says that she supports a “moratorium on new large-scale projects until clear guardrails are established”. She also supports economic incentives on data centers and will be harsh on them if certain standards are not met, mentioned in her plan. It states that if data centers do not meet New Mexico’s energy and zero-carbon requirements then there will be “restrictions on economic incentives”. She also mentions that data centers will adhere to “noise limits” so they don’t harm New Mexico’s environment, per her eight point plan.

name: Greggory Hull
summary: Greggory Hull is a New Mexican politician who served as mayor of Rio Rancho from 2024 to 2025. He is also the Republican nominee for the Governor of New Mexico. He has expressed his approval of separate utility rates for data centers. Hull said that he would “never support” and raise utility rates, per KOB 4. Contrary to Haaland, Hull does not support a statewide moratorium on data centers. He said that he doesn’t want to “send a nationwide message that New Mexico is closed for business by putting moratoriums on certain industries”, per KUNM. He mentioned how when he was mayor of Rio Rancho he turned down economic development deals because they “didn’t fit our community” and that in these situations New Mexico has a right to say no. He also supports business incentives for data centers and said that without them “data centers likely wouldn’t want to set up shop in New Mexico”, per KOB 4. He has not said whether he supports noise assessment requirements for proposed data centers and public reporting requirements for water use.

name: Kathy Hochul
moratorim-link to source: https://www.governor.ny.gov/executive-order/no-62-establishing-temporary-moratorium-data-centers-new-york-while-state-develops -- Hochul's office has branded this as the first statewide data center moratorium in the country; it contains answers to all but one of the remaining questions here.
summary: Kathy Hochul is the incumbent Democratic governor of New York. She has been outspoken on the issue of data centers, issuing an executive order in July 2026 that established a one-year moratorium on state-level permitting for data centers. The executive order calls for separate utility rates and use requirements for data centers, and for noise assessment requirements for proposed data centers. It additionally advocates against tax incentives for data centers. Hochul’s campaign did not respond when asked whether or not the candidate supports public reporting requirements for water use.

name: Bruce Blakeman
summary: Bruce Blakeman is the Republican candidate for governor of New York. He is currently the county executive of Nassau County, on Long Island. Blakeman’s campaign did not respond to emails asking his position on data centers, but the candidate has been outspoken against Hochul’s data center moratorium. In July 2026, he called the moratorium “crazy” and said that Hochul “should have had it figured out by now.” Blakeman has also indicated that he believes data centers are essential to maintaining New York’s competitive advantage with other states.

name: Amy Aciton
summary: Amy Acton, Democratic challenger for Ohio governor; former Ohio Department of Health director, Supports a conditional moratorium and requiring data centers to pay 100% of their utility costs; supports tighter conditions on environmental, labor and community impacts

name: Vivek Ramaswamy
summary: Vivek Ramaswamy, Republican challenger for Ohio governor; businessman/biotech entrepreneur, Supports a temporary halt on new approvals until his requirements are enacted; wants data centers to pay full property taxes, cover nearby residents' electricity costs, recycle/minimize water and meet environmental standards.

name: Cyndi Munson
summary: Cyndi Munson is the Democratic candidate and challenger for governor of Oklahoma. She currently serves as the minority leader in the Oklahoma House of Representatives. She stated in the 2026 Oklahoma Governor's Debate that she supports developing a stronger and standardized statewide approach that would help protect Oklahoma's water resources. She also backs separate utility treatment for large data centers. Munson helped coauthor and voted for Oklahoma HB 2992, which would require separate tariffs for large-load customers. She has also stated that she would impose a moratorium on new data center projects on her first day in office to "set guidelines and keep big tech companies accountable when building these data centers." Munson also opposes tax incentives, stating that data centers should not receive taxpayer funds. She has not said whether she supports noise assessment requirements.

name: Mike Mazzei
summary: Mike Mazzei is the Republican candidate and challenger in the race for governor of Oklahoma. He is currently the chairman and CEO of Trinity Strategic Wealth. According to the News On 6 voter guide, Mazzei supports separate utility rates and usage rules for data centers, requiring them to provide their own electricity and cooling systems. He has not endorsed a statewide moratorium. Alternatively, he says data centers must meet these four conditions: no taxpayer funding, paying their own electricity costs without increasing other customers’ rates, locally approved industrial sites, and advanced closed-loop cooling systems. Mazzei opposes special-interest property tax breaks for data centers and has proposed to eliminate them and use that recovered revenue as property tax relief for senior citizens and veterans. He has not stated his position on noise assessment or public water reporting requirements.

name: Tina Kotek
summary: Tina Kotek is the incumbent governor of Oregon, a position she has held since 2023. She has been in public office since she was elected in 2006, later serving as the speaker of Oregon's House of Representatives. Oregon has the ninth most data centers in the nation as of February, and Kotek has said she supports prohibiting all new data center development until new state standards are in place. In 2025 she supported the state's POWER Act, which placed the costs of large energy users solely on the consumers, rather than families and other businesses.

name: Christine Drazan
summary: Sen. Chistrine Drazan is the Republican challenger in Oregon's gubernatorial race. Drazan currently represents Oregon's 26th Senate district and has held that position for a year. Drazan ran for governor in 2022, served in the state House in 2019 and worked as chief of staff for Oregon House Speaker Mark Simmons in 2001. She has said she will protect communities from unwanted data center development, later saying that she supports a statewide moratorium. If she wins, she will be the state's first Republican governor in 40 years.

name: Josh Shapiro
tax-link to source: https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/governor/documents/eo2026_05_protecting%20pennsylvania%20consumers%20from%20data%20center%20impacts_final_executed.pdf (incentives are to ensure the data centers are environmentally concious)
summary: Josh Shapiro is Pennsylvania's incumbent governor, having served since 2023. Pennsylvania enacted a tax break for data centers in 2021, but in August, Shapiro made this tax break contingent on following certain guidelines. He does not support a moratorium on data centers, but he does support public reporting for water use, a noise assessment for proposed data centers and having the data centers produce and pay for their utility usage. Shapiro signed an executive order in August that is widely regarded as having the strictest data center rules because data centers have to receive local support and adhere to environmental regulations.

name: Stacy Garrity
water-link to source: https://www.wgal.com/article/pa-stacy-garrity-priorities-stance-on-key-issues/73772839 (She wants them to find their own water and energy sources)
summary: Stacy Garrity is the Republican opponent in the Pennsylvania gubernatorial race; she is currently the state's treasurer. Garrity supports strict controls on data centers with required water reporting, separate utility rates and the removal of tax incentives for data centers. Garrity has called for data centers to produce their own energy and get their water from a different supply than residents. Additionally, she is supporting a temporary moratorium on data centers until Pennsylvanians and government officials can have a conversation and determine how to proceed.

name: Helena Buonanno Foulkes
summary: Helena Foulkes is the Democratic candidate for governor of Rhode Island. She defeated the incumbent governor Dan McKee in September's primary. Foulkes supports regulation of data centers as opposed to an outright moratorium. She has stated she is in favor of measures being taken to offset increased utility costs for residents, but has not outlined a particular strategy. Foulkes was formerly an executive at Hudson's Bay and CVS.

name: Aaron Guckian
summary: Aaron Guckian is the Republican candidate for governor of Rhode Island. Guckian has previously stated he is in favor of municipalities self determining whether or not they construct data centers. Guckian supports public reporting requirements for water use, separate utility rates for data centers and noise assessment requirements, but does not want a state moratorium on data center construction. He does not support tax incentives for data centers, except under very specific circumstances . "Only when there is a clear, measurable benefit to Rhode Island taxpayers. I'm not interested in handing out tax breaks simply because a company promises to invest here," Guckian said in an email. "We need to know what we're getting in return, including permanent jobs, economic activity and a positive return on any public investment. Incentives should be earned, not assumed."

name: Ken Block
summary: Ken Block is the independent candidate for governor of Rhode Island. He has long been a prominent figure in Rhode Island 3rd party politics, having founded the Moderate Party of Rhode Island. His platform has primarily focused on preventing increases in taxes and opposing wasteful spending in government.

name: Jermaine Johnson
summary: Dr. Jermaine Johnson is currently running for governor as a sitting Democrat in the South Carolina House of Representatives. In April, Johnson began pushing an initiative through the legislature that would put a moratorium on all data center construction. He is still pushing for this initiative, prioritizing his "BYOE," bring your own energy, to data center corporations. Stated in a Facebook post, Johnson said "before we move forward, we need a responsible, transparent plan that protects our communities, infrastructure, and energy resources."

name: Alan Wilson
summary: Alan Wilson is the current attorney general in South Carolina. Endorsed by President Trump, Wilson is running on a large conservative platform. He believes that anything regarding data centers should be left to the local populations rather than instating broader laws for the entire state.

name: Dan Ahlers
summary: Dan Ahlers is the Democratic candidate for Governor of South Dakota. He’s lived in Dell Rapids for over 20 years, where he served as President of the Haven Before and After School Program, the Dell Rapids Chamber of Commerce, and the Dell Rapids Community Fund. He’s represented District 25 in the State Legislature for the past 6 years, and believes in supporting rural South Dakota, supporting education infrastructure and funding, affordable housing, expanding rural healthcare, and livable wages.

name: Larry Rhoden
summary: Larry Rhoden is the Republican candidate and incumbent running for Governor of South Dakota. Formerly a rancher and welder from Union Center, he began his work in public office as a school board member, then became a state legislator and Lieutenant Governor under former Governor Kristi Noem and was elevated to Governor after her resignation in 2025. Rhoden states that he believes in low taxes, strong property rights, and maintaining personal freedoms, including the Second Amendment.

name: Jerri Green
summary: Jerri Green is a Democratic candidate for governor of Tennessee and a Memphis City Council member running as a challenger. Green supports a statewide moratorium on new data centers and says she would work to stop state incentives for their construction. She has called for stronger standards addressing data centers' water use, energy demand, environmental impacts, infrastructure costs, zoning and community input. Green says data-center companies should pay their share of infrastructure costs rather than passing those costs on to Tennessee families, and her campaign proposes requiring tech companies to use recycled water to cool servers. However, her published positions do not specifically state whether she supports public reporting requirements for water use, separate utility rates or required noise assessments for proposed data centers.

name: Marsha Blackburn
summary: Marsha Blackburn is a Republican candidate for governor of Tennessee and a challenger who currently serves as a U.S. senator representing Tennessee. Blackburn has said data centers will be an important part of Tennessee's economic growth but has called for thoughtful placement, including opposing a proposed data center next to the Nashville Zoo. She supports protections intended to prevent data-center energy and infrastructure costs from being passed on to other utility customers and has supported disclosure of expected water use and potential community impacts. Her public positions support continued data-center development rather than a statewide moratorium. No clear position was found on whether she supports tax incentives specifically for data centers or required noise assessments for proposed facilities.

name: Gina Hinojosa
summary: Gina Hinojosa is a Democratic candidate and challenger for govenor in the 2026 election. She is currently in her fifth term in the Texas House and previously served on the Austin Independent School District Board.  Hinojosa wants stronger rules and regulations to protect Texas from data center. She wants to temporarily stop new data centers until stronger protections are created. She wants companies to be more transparent about how much water and electricity they are using and make sure families and the community are not paying for those bills. Hinojosa wants to stop the tax breaks that is happening and give the community more voice and say where these data centers are going.

name: Greg Abbott
summary: Greg Abbott is a Republican incumbent currently the governor of Texas, running for reelection to a fourth term in 2026. He has been governor since 2015 and previously served as the attorney general, and Texas Supreme Court justice. Abbott wants companies to take more responisbility for the impact and cost of data centers, he wants Texas State officals to review how these data centers are affecting water use, electricity, traffic, and communtities in Texas. Abbott has not called for a state wide ban on data centers but he has supported a temporarypause on certain data center approvals and permits while the state checks audits. He wants to inforce data centers to pay for electricty systems instead of making everyday electricty customers pay the cost. He has also said he wants to deminish data centers from recieving tax breaks and wants to inforce stricter rules to help solve things like water use and noise.

name: Amanda Janoo
summary: Amanda Janoo is the Democrat challenger running for Governor of Vermont. Janoo is from rural Vermont and grew up in a working class, bi-racial family. For the past two decades Janoo has worked with governments and communities to implement strategies that create good jobs, strengthen local businesses, reduce inequalities, and build reselient local economies. Janoo's goal is to ensure all Vermonters are safe and secure in current times of crisis whether that's economically, politically or environmentally.

name: Phil Scott
summary: Phil Scott is the incumbent Republican Governor of Vermont. Scott is a native of Vermont and prior to becoming Governor, he was a small business owner and a race car driver. Scott wants to prioritize helping the economy grow, making Vermont more affordable and protecting those who are most vulnerable. A voluntary paid family and medical leave program was launched by Scott to give all employed Vermonters access to affordable paid family and medical leave insurance.

name: David Crowley
summary: David Crowley is the Democratic incumbent governor of State. He has expressed disapproval for a statewide moratorium on data centers because he wants to call for stricter regulations governing how the developments may move forward. He supports public water reporting requirements for data centers of any size as well as separate utility rates and use requirements for data centers. In 2023, David led the passage of Wisconsin Act 12,  a landmark bipartisan bill to increase shared revenue for municipalities and counties across Wisconsin. He also signed into law the largest property tax cut in Milwaukee County history. Crowley has not said whether he supports noise assessment requirements for data centers.

name: Tom Tiffany
summary: Tom Tiffany is the Republican incumbent governor of State. He has expressed disapproval for a statewide moratorium on data centers because he wants to call for stricter regulations governing how the developments may move forward. He does not support separate utility rates and use requirements for data centers. In his six years of service,Tom Tiffany has focused on strengthening rural economies, supporting Second Amendment rights, and promoting energy independence. Tiffany has not said whether he supports noise assessment requirements for data centers or water reporting requirements.

name: Ken Casner
summary: Ken Casner is the Democratic candidate for the Governor of Wyoming. Casner has not publicly disclosed topics and issues surrounding datacenters for Wyoming. When asked aout AI he said, “It's a tool. It's in a box. That's what it is. It's a toolbox. That's my feeling with it, because basically it helps in certain areas, but it's a disadvantage in another.” Casner has supported universal healthcare and his number one issue is free and open elections. According to Casner, his political beliefs stem directly from following the Constitution of the United States.

name: Eric Barlow
summary: Eric Barlow is the Republican candidate for the Governor of Wyoming. Barlow has not explicitly stated his stance on tax incentives or noise assessments for datacenters, but he does focus on the management of local resources for the datacenters. As he is not in favor of a statewide moratorium for datacenters, Barlow thinks Wyoming could benefit from datacenters. “It will be using Wyoming energy, if it’s in Wyoming … and minimal or no Wyoming water,” Barlow said. “Technology solves a lot of things.” Barlow is focused on having a limited government, robust economy and thriving communities.
